Chapter Two: The Roots of Death Anxiety and the Birth of the Hero
Think back to when you were a kid. There’s that special mix of wonder and fear—the world feels magical, sure, but it’s also a little bit terrifying, isn’t it? Picture a young person lying awake at night, not just worried about the shadows in the corner, but quietly wondering what happens when the lights go out for good. Not just in the room... but in life itself.
It’s not just about monsters under the bed. It’s really our first brush with the idea that everything—even who we are—could suddenly... disappear.
As we get older, we learn to push those fears away. Parents and teachers tell us to be brave. They share stories of heroes—those unforgettable people who face danger and come out stronger. But have you noticed? These stories aren’t just for fun. They actually teach us how to deal with fear itself.
The hero becomes this guiding star—a symbol of what it means to stand up to the unknown, to make a difference, and to be remembered. The message is simple, but powerful: if you want to matter, if you want to be more than just another face in the crowd, you need to conquer the fear of being forgotten.
And in real life, this drive shows up all over the place. Think about the student who stays up late, pouring over books, hoping for that one bit of praise that sets them apart. Or the artist who pours their soul into a piece, dreaming it’ll last long after they’re gone. Even a parent, making sacrifices for their children, hoping to leave behind a legacy of love.
Every one of those actions is a way of reaching for meaning... trying to prove that life, somehow, matters.
But here’s something to pay attention to—underneath all this striving, there’s a deeper struggle. The knowledge that one day, we won’t be here, creates this tension. We all want to believe we’re special, that our lives have meaning that’s bigger than just getting through the day. That hope feels good, but it’s also kind of fragile. Because when things don’t work out, or when nobody notices our efforts, those old fears come creeping back in.
Our whole society actually encourages this quest for heroism. Just look around—awards, honors, that moment of public recognition... all held up as proof that you matter. Even the little things, like getting likes on a photo, a compliment at work, or a small promotion. We all crave that reassurance. And sure, those moments feel amazing—but they rarely last. The need for validation just keeps coming back.
For some people, comfort comes from faith or spiritual beliefs—the idea that life goes on even after death. The promise of immortality, whether it’s real or just symbolic, can be a powerful way to calm those fears. Rituals, prayers, and shared beliefs help us feel like we belong to something bigger, something eternal. And honestly, that sense of connection can be a real source of strength when we’re facing uncertainty.
Others look for meaning by investing in causes or communities. Maybe they volunteer, donate, or fight for change—because deep down, they hope their actions will outlast them. It’s about building something that endures, making sure their life has purpose.
But chasing heroism can have a dark side, too. When the need to be special takes over, it can turn into anxiety, jealousy, or even anger. People start competing for recognition, feeling bitter when someone else gets the spotlight, or crushed when they fall short. That fear of being insignificant? It can push folks into risky choices, just to prove themselves.
And sometimes, trying to deny death means denying our own vulnerability. People act like nothing scares them, hiding their fears and weaknesses behind a mask. But keeping up that act is exhausting. It can leave you feeling isolated—like you have to be strong all the time, and asking for help just isn’t an option.
So, what’s the answer? It’s all about finding balance. We want to matter, to make a difference, but we can’t let the fear of mortality run our lives. Most of us don’t even realize how much this struggle shapes what we do. The drive to be a hero, to leave a mark, can be a wonderful thing—but it can also be a trap.
The first step? Just recognizing how these forces are at play. That awareness opens the door to living with more honesty, more compassion, and a little less fear.
